AmIMotion makes the tags, the anchors and the software that show where work is in a plant, and where it waits. One team builds all three. AmIMotion is spatial intelligence for factories and warehouses. It is a brand of Locatepro Technologies Pvt Ltd, Bengaluru, India. AmIMotion designs and builds AmIGo tags, AmIMo anchors and AmIHub software, on NXP Trimension UWB silicon. It is built on the FiRa and omlox specifications. AmIMotion is led by Kaushal Kukkar, founder and CEO, and Vivek Dham, CTO. What is AmIMotion? · How to buy Who leads it. AmIMotion is led by Kaushal Kukkar, founder and CEO, and Vivek Dham, CTO. AmIMotion is a brand of Locatepro Technologies Pvt Ltd, Bengaluru, India. The tags, the anchors and AmIHub are designed and built in India, with local stock and local engineers on your site. What we make. AmIGo tag Rides on what moves. Sends a short UWB pulse when it moves and sleeps when it stops. AmIMo anchor Hears every tag. Fixed to a column or wall, it needs only power. AmIHub One live map. Runs on an industrial PC inside your plant, with no internet needed. How we work. One team, every layer AmIMotion designs the tags, the anchors and AmIHub. One contract and one support line cover every layer. Made in India Designed and built in India, with local stock and local engineers on your site. Open by design Built on the FiRa and omlox specifications. AmIHub connects through open REST, MQTT, WebSocket and omlox hub interfaces, so your team or your integrator can build on it. One bay first Every AmIMotion pilot starts with one bay or line. Then it grows plant-wide on the same AmIHub, without re-fitting the first bay. What we will not claim. A position is only useful when you know what it can and cannot tell you. A position shows where a trolley is, and AmIHub says when it was last seen. It does not show which job the trolley carries until that job is linked to it. It does not say why work waited. That is for your team to say. This site names no customer and shows no customer result. Five ways into AmIHub. AmIHub keeps one record of where each tag is and when it moved. Your code reads it over open interfaces, inside your plant or in the cloud. AmIHub , AmIMotion's software, gives developers location data over REST, MQTT, WebSocket and an omlox hub interface, and has an MCP server built in for AI assistants. Every interface runs over TLS, with API keys and access by role, and every call is logged. On-premise, AmIHub runs on a PC inside your plant, so every interface stays on your network. Specifications · Trust and data What you can read. Records, not raw radio. Positions A 3D position for every tracked item, with the time AmIHub saw it. Zone events Each entry, exit, idle and dwell, with the tag, the zone and the time stamps. History Trails, trips and waits for any item, over the time window you ask for. CSV and Parquet export. Devices Health, battery level and firmware state for each AmIGo tag and AmIMo anchor. The map Your floor plan, zones, fences and racking. Trackables Assets, vehicles and work orders are objects in AmIHub. You assign tags to them, in AmIHub or over the API. Pick the interface. By what your system needs. Interface Pattern Use it for REST Request and response Queries from MES, ERP, WMS and BI tools MQTT Publish and subscribe Zone events into plant systems, as they happen WebSocket Live stream Screens and your own apps that show live positions omlox hub interface The open omlox location model Data that is not tied to one vendor's format MCP server Tools for AI assistants Questions in plain words; any change needs a person's approval Which topics, fields and rates your systems receive is agreed for your site. The architecture for your site comes with the datasheets, under NDA. A zone event, in words. T-114 entered Inspection at 09:12 . { "tag" : "T-114" , "zone" : "Inspection" , "event" : "entered" , "time" : "09:12:04" } Example. Field names for your site come with the datasheets. When a tagged trolley enters a zone, AmIHub records an event. It names the tag, the zone, the kind of event (entered, left, idle or dwell) and the time. When the trolley leaves, a second event closes the visit, so the wait is the time between them. You can take these events as they happen over MQTT or WebSocket, or ask AmIHub for them by time window over REST. Link each trolley to the job it carries, in AmIHub or from your own system. AmIHub then reports the wait against that job. Your MES stays in charge of the job itself. AI assistants, with limits. AmIHub has an MCP server built in. MCP is an open standard that lets AI assistants use other software. Scoped Each assistant gets its own access: read-only, or only the actions you allow. Logged Every request is logged: who asked, what was called and what changed. Approved Any change, such as raising a work order, needs a person's approval. You can require it from a supervisor. AmIHub's MCP tools cover live positions, history by time window, zones and fences, and the tags assigned to things. The same tools are there over REST and MQTT. Short answers, with their conditions. AmIMotion makes AmIGo tags, AmIMo anchors and AmIHub software, designed and built in India by Locatepro Technologies in Bengaluru. Together they give each tagged trolley, bin, tool and vehicle a time-stamped location, down to ±10 cm in 3D with AmIMo anchors, depending on the site. The answers below cover the company, the three parts, accuracy, cabling, data, standards and AI assistants. The company. What is AmIMotion? AmIMotion builds industrial spatial intelligence for factories and warehouses. AmIMotion makes AmIGo UWB tags, AmIMo anchors and AmIHub software. AmIMotion is a brand of Locatepro Technologies Pvt Ltd in Bengaluru, and its products are designed and built in India. What does AmIMotion do? AmIMotion shows where work is and where it waits. A small AmIGo tag rides on each trolley, bin and tool in a factory or warehouse. AmIMo anchors hear it, and AmIHub's live map shows where it went and how long it has waited. Who makes AmIMotion and where is it based? Locatepro Technologies Pvt Ltd, in Bengaluru, India. AmIMotion is its brand, and the tags, anchors and software are designed and built in India. Who leads AmIMotion? AmIMotion is led by Kaushal Kukkar, founder and CEO, and Vivek Dham, CTO. What does AmIMotion cost? After the first call, we share datasheets, architecture, prices and pilot options under NDA. Can we start small? Yes. An AmIMotion pilot starts in one bay or one line. You then scale on the same AmIHub. The three parts. What is an AmIGo tag? AmIGo is AmIMotion's UWB tag. An AmIGo tag rides on a trolley, bin, tool or vehicle, wakes on motion and sleeps when still. Battery life is 1 to 3 years, typical and usage-dependent. What is an AmIMo anchor? AmIMo is AmIMotion's UWB anchor. An AmIMo anchor mounts on a column or wall, times each tag's pulse and measures the angle it came from. Each anchor syncs over the air, sends data over Wi-Fi with an Ethernet option, and needs power from a DC adapter or PoE. What is AmIHub? AmIHub is AmIMotion's software. AmIHub works out positions, keeps the live map and zone history, and offers REST, MQTT, WebSocket, an omlox hub interface and a built-in MCP server. AmIHub runs on-premise with no internet dependency, or in the cloud. How it works. How accurate is AmIMotion? Down to ±10 cm in 3D, typical, with AmIMo anchors. Accuracy depends on the site, so a pilot measures it on your floor. Do the anchors need cables? No data or sync cabling. AmIMo anchors sync over the air and send data over Wi-Fi, with an Ethernet option. Each anchor needs power, from a DC adapter or PoE. Does UWB work in a factory full of steel and racking? UWB's wide bandwidth separates the direct signal from reflections. AmIHub adds multipath and non-line-of-sight algorithms, and AmIMotion plans the anchors from a site survey. How long do tag batteries last? 1 to 3 years, typical and usage-dependent. AmIGo tags sleep when still and send when they move. Does AmIMotion track individual parts? AmIMotion tags the carrier: the trolley, bin or rack. Which parts or job it holds comes from a carrier-to-job link, not from the radio. Systems, data and AI. Can it run without the internet? Yes. AmIHub can run on an industrial PC inside your plant with no internet dependency, or in the cloud. Does it connect to our MES or ERP? AmIHub offers REST, MQTT, WebSocket and an omlox hub interface, and can push events to MES, ERP, WMS, SCADA or BI. Connectors are confirmed for each site. Does AmIMotion hold FiRa or omlox certification? AmIMotion is built on the FiRa and omlox specifications. AmIMotion claims no formal certification. Does AmIMotion have an MCP server for AI assistants? Yes. AmIHub has a built-in MCP server, so MCP-capable AI assistants can query live positions, zones and history. Any change needs a person's approval, and every call is logged. AmIMotion shows it in a live demo. Ask us the next one. AmIMotion's films show one model factory floor from above. Blue lines show where tagged trolleys, tools and vehicles went. Amber marks the trolleys and pallets that are waiting. The first film runs nine seconds: the same floor before and after AmIMotion, from scan ticks at three desks to every path and wait on one live map. What you are looking at. Blue Where a tagged thing went. An AmIGo tag sends a short UWB pulse as it moves, and AmIMo anchors on the columns hear it. Amber Where work waits. AmIHub notes when each trolley or pallet enters a zone and when it leaves, so you see a wait while it is still a wait. Pale Everything nobody has tagged. The nine seconds, in words. The film opens on the floor as AmIMotion shows it. Blue trails run behind every moving thing: the tugger's train, the forklift, an AMR, a trolley leaving the press. Three trolleys in the inspection queue and one pallet in the staging lane stand on amber. At two seconds the colour goes. This is the floor as most plants see it. At three checkpoint desks, a short blue tick appears as a trolley passes. Nothing marks the path between desks. One trolley passes a desk, turns behind the racks and stops. No mark follows it. Then the ticks join into lines, one kind of thing at a time: trolleys, bins and a fixture, the tool cart, the forklift and tugger, the AMR. The three trolleys and the pallet take their amber again. At nine seconds the frame is back where it began. The same stories, on their own pages. Where is that trolley? The one that turned behind the racks. Floor words and tech words, in plain English. 39 terms you will hear when people talk about location on a factory floor. AmIMotion's glossary defines the words used in real-time location on factory floors, from RTLS and UWB to dwell time and carrier-to-job links. Each term has a plain definition, and where a term names an AmIMotion part, the definition says so. AmIMo anchors locate AmIGo tags down to ±10 cm in 3D, depending on the site. RTLS UWB Tag Anchor Time of flight TWR TDoA UL-TDoA DL-TDoA AoA Multipath NLOS Over-the-air sync Wi-Fi FTM BLE ranging Update rate Site survey PoE IEEE 802.15.4z FiRa omlox Certification WIP WIP visibility Carrier Association Zone Geofence Dwell Exception Last seen Freshness MES, ERP, WMS AGV and AMR Milk run AmIHub MCP Industrial spatial intelligence Edge Positioning RTLS Real-time location system: fixed infrastructure and software that continuously locate tagged objects, usually indoors where GPS does not work. AmIMotion is a UWB RTLS. UWB Ultra-wideband: radio that sends very short pulses across a wide band of frequencies. Short pulses allow precise timing, so distance can be measured to centimetres and echoes told apart. Tag The small device fixed to whatever is tracked: a carrier, tool or vehicle. AmIMotion's tag is AmIGo, which wakes on motion and lasts 1 to 3 years on its battery, typical and usage-dependent. Anchor A fixed device at a known position that receives UWB signals from tags. AmIMotion's anchor is AmIMo, a UWB anchor with a 3D angle-of-arrival antenna array. AmIMo needs power from a DC adapter or PoE, and no data or sync cabling. Time of flight The time a radio signal takes to travel from transmitter to receiver. Multiplied by the speed of light, about 30 cm per nanosecond, it gives distance. TWR Two-way ranging: tag and anchor exchange messages and measure the round trip to work out the distance. TDoA Time difference of arrival: a position worked out from the differences in when one signal reaches several synchronised anchors. UL-TDoA Uplink TDoA: the tag sends a short blink and the anchors work out its position. Tags only transmit, so many low-power tags can be tracked. DL-TDoA Downlink TDoA: anchors transmit and the device works out its own position, like GPS indoors. AoA Angle of arrival: an antenna array measures the direction a signal comes from. 3D AoA measures the horizontal and the vertical angle. Multipath Copies of a signal that arrive late after bouncing off metal, walls or racking. NLOS Non-line-of-sight: the direct path between tag and anchor is blocked, so the strongest signal may be a reflection. Over-the-air sync Keeping anchor clocks in step by radio instead of timing cables. AmIMo anchors sync over the air. Wi-Fi FTM Fine Timing Measurement (IEEE 802.11mc): Wi-Fi round-trip timing that lets compatible Wi-Fi devices estimate distance without a separate tag. BLE ranging Estimating distance to Bluetooth Low Energy devices. Usually coarse, at room or zone level. Update rate How often a tag reports. 0.1 Hz is once every 10 seconds; 10 Hz is ten times a second. Site survey A visit that maps ceiling height, racking, metal and sight lines before anchors go up. AmIMotion sets the final anchor count from a site survey. PoE Power over Ethernet: power delivered over a network cable. An AmIMo anchor can take its power by PoE or from a DC adapter. Standards IEEE 802.15.4z The UWB standard amendment that adds enhanced and secure ranging. HRP is the high-rate pulse physical layer used by most current UWB chips. FiRa The FiRa Consortium, an industry body that defines interoperable UWB specifications and runs certification programmes. omlox An open standard for interoperable industrial location systems, so different location technologies and vendors can feed one location hub. Certification A formal certification means an authorised body has tested a product against a specification. Following a specification is a company's own statement. AmIMotion describes itself as built on the FiRa and omlox specifications. Operations WIP Work in progress: partly finished goods moving through production. WIP visibility Knowing where work in progress physically is, which job each carrier holds and how long it has waited in each zone. Carrier The trolley, bin, rack or container that holds WIP. In a WIP visibility system the carrier carries the tag. Association The link between a tagged carrier and the job it holds, which gives a location its work meaning. A link needs a start, an end and an owner. Zone An agreed area of the floor, such as an assembly queue. Entering or leaving it creates a time-stamped event. Geofence A boundary drawn on the floor map. Crossing it creates an event, in the same way as a zone. Dwell Time spent in a zone, from entry to exit. Dwell includes waiting, processing and breaks, so it is not the same as cycle time. Exception A case that asks a person to look, such as work that has waited longer than the team agreed. An exception is not a diagnosis. Last seen The last place and time a tag was located. An honest map shows a quiet tag as last seen, never as live. Freshness How old a position is when someone uses it. A precise position can still be too old to act on. MES, ERP, WMS Manufacturing execution, enterprise resource planning and warehouse management systems: the systems of record for jobs, orders and stock. AGV and AMR Automated guided vehicle, which follows fixed paths, and autonomous mobile robot, which navigates freely. Milk run A fixed delivery loop, often by tugger, that feeds line-side stations. Software and AI AmIHub AmIMotion's software. AmIHub works out positions and keeps the live map, zones, time-stamped events and interfaces: REST, MQTT, WebSocket, an omlox hub interface and a built-in MCP server. AmIHub runs on a PC inside your plant with no internet dependency, or in the cloud. MCP Model Context Protocol: an open standard that lets AI assistants use external tools and data. AmIHub has a built-in MCP server. Industrial spatial intelligence A time-stamped location for what moves in a plant, joined with context such as jobs and zones, so people, systems and AI assistants can answer where work is and where it waits. Edge Computing done on site, near the equipment, rather than in a remote cloud. Read next. What is RTLS? Real-time location, plainly. What is WIP visibility? Where each job is, and how long it waited. Questions Short answers about AmIMotion. Questions about your own floor? An engineer answers them on a short call, with the live map open. A field guide What is spatial intelligence? Industrial spatial intelligence is a time-stamped location for every trolley, bin, tool and vehicle you tag in a factory or warehouse, joined with your zones and with the jobs each carrier holds. With it, people, plant systems and AI assistants can answer where work is and where it waits. AmIMotion builds it, on UWB positioning down to ±10 cm in 3D with AmIMo anchors, depending on the floor. One answer. On its own, a location is a dot on a map. Spatial intelligence adds what the dot means, one layer at a time. 1 Location Where each tagged thing is, to the centimetre, and when it was seen there. AmIGo tags and AmIMo anchors measure it over UWB. 2 Context The zones you draw and the job each carrier holds. Now the dot is a job's trolley, standing at inspection. 3 Answer Time does the rest: how long it has stood there. Supervisors read it on AmIHub , your MES and ERP read it over open interfaces, and AI assistants ask it over MCP. 3 · Answer Bay 1 · 09:17:04 One answer, taken apart. Every field has a source. This is what AmIHub holds about one trolley at one moment. The first fields come from the radio. The next come from you. The last is worked out from both, and nothing in it is guessed. Measured by AmIGo and AmIMo over UWB, whenever the trolley moves Given by you: the zones on your floor plan, and the link from tag to job Worked out by AmIHub, from the two above and the clock amihub · record Example tag T-114 x, y, z 20.00, 5.43, 0.92 m seen 09:17:04.312 zone Inspection job Your job number from your MES entered 08:36:10 state waiting for 41 min How it differs. RTLS Where is it? Spatial intelligence Where is work waiting, and for how long? If a record at each checkpoint is all you need, a scan is enough. AmIMotion is for the time between checkpoints. What location alone cannot tell you. And who answers instead. Which job A tag names the trolley, not the job on it. You link each trolley to its job , in AmIHub or from your own system. How accurate is UWB? Test it where your floor is hardest. What a quoted figure means, and how to measure it on your own floor. UWB can tell neighbouring lanes and queues apart when its anchors are planned for it. AmIMotion quotes down to ±10 cm in 3D with AmIMo anchors. The figure is typical, and the real one depends on the site. UWB's very short pulses let the direct signal be told apart from reflections off steel racking and forklifts. A pilot should still measure accuracy in the hardest places on your floor, with the method agreed in advance. Agree what you measure Include the hard places Steel, racking and forklifts Measure data age separately End with a person Agree what you measure Ask what “typical” means for your setup, how true positions will be measured, and how the spread of errors will be reported. Typical is the usual case, not every point. If your process needs a stricter figure, agree it in writing with AmIMotion or any supplier before the pilot. Include the hard places Test near metal, behind racking, at awkward mounting spots, near forklifts, and with tags both moving and still. Note where coverage is expected and where the system should admit doubt. Name these spots in the AmIMotion pilot plan before the anchors go up. Steel, racking and forklifts Racking and machines bounce radio around. UWB's wide band separates the direct path from the echoes, and AmIHub adds multipath and non-line-of-sight algorithms to keep positions stable around racking, metal and moving vehicles. Dense racking may still need more anchors, or anchors that see down each aisle. AmIMotion sets the anchor plan from a site survey. Measure data age separately Record when each position was seen, when it was received and when someone used it. A fast system can still show old data if a tag reports slowly. AmIGo tags report at a rate set per tag group, from 0.1 to 10 times a second, so set a freshness target for each task. End with a person Give a supervisor a real task. Can they find the right trolley and its job, and see how old the position is? Record how much they had to correct. The figure that matters is whether the AmIMotion map sends them to the right place. Common follow-ups. Is UWB accurate enough to track trolleys in a factory? Usually, yes, when anchors are planned for the floor. AmIMotion locates tags down to ±10 cm in 3D with AmIMo anchors, typical and site-dependent, which is enough to tell neighbouring lanes and queues apart. Measure it on your floor in a pilot. Does UWB work around steel racking and forklifts? UWB's very short pulses separate the direct signal from reflections off steel, and AmIHub adds multipath and non-line-of-sight handling. Dense racking can need extra anchors, which a site survey shows. Does ±10 cm mean every reading is within 10 cm? No. Down to ±10 cm is typical with AmIMo anchors in good conditions. A pilot reports the spread of errors on your floor. Is the ±10 cm figure 2D or 3D? 3D, typical, with AmIMo anchors. AmIHub works out each position in 3D from pulse timing and the anchors' 3D angle of arrival. Read next. How many UWB anchors? What really sets the count. Scan, checkpoint or location? Each one answers a different question. How to decide what your flow needs, before you buy anything. Start with the question. Do you need a person to confirm a step, proof that something passed a point, or where it is right now? A barcode scan confirms a step. An RFID checkpoint proves passage without a person. UWB location, such as AmIMotion, shows where work is between those points and how long it waits, down to ±10 cm in 3D with AmIMo anchors, depending on the site. Many plants keep their scans and add location only where work goes quiet. Side by side When a scan is right When a checkpoint is enough When location adds something Compare the whole effort Use the same test Side by side Barcode scan RFID checkpoint UWB location Who acts A person scans Nobody, at the read point Nobody What you learn A step is confirmed An item passed this point Where it is, where it went, how long it waited Between points Nothing Nothing Continuous position What you install Scanners and labels Reader antennas at each point Anchors on columns, planned from a site survey When a scan is right A scan is a deliberate confirmation of an item or a step, such as a quality check. If that is all your process needs, improve the scanning first. AmIMotion does not replace a scan that confirms a step. When a checkpoint is enough If you only need to know that an item passed a point, such as a dock door, test an RFID checkpoint against exactly that. A checkpoint answers a passage question well. When location adds something If work moves between scans and people go looking for it, location answers a new question. With AmIMotion, AmIHub shows where each tagged trolley was last seen and how long it has waited in each zone. Location still needs a link to the job and a tested installation. Compare the whole effort Count everything: anchors or readers, the survey, power, network, tag mounting, reassigning tags, upkeep and the exceptions people handle by hand. Compare the cost of useful answers, not hardware prices alone. AmIMo anchors need power from a DC adapter or PoE, and no data or sync cabling. Use the same test Give every option the same scenario and the same measures. Record what each one sees, what it misses and how much human effort it needs. Run the same test on AmIMotion in a one-bay pilot. Common follow-ups. Do we have to replace barcode scanning? No. Keep scans where a person must confirm a step. AmIMotion adds location where work moves and waits between scans. When is RFID the better choice? When you need proof that items passed fixed points, such as dock doors, and nothing in between. How do we compare the options fairly? Give each one the same scenario, the same measures and the same time on the floor, then compare what each saw and missed. Read next. UWB, BLE or RFID? How many UWB anchors? Fewer than area suggests, more than racking allows. What sets the count, a worked example, and where the real number comes from. No honest formula gives an anchor count from floor area alone. The count depends on the accuracy you need, 2D or 3D, the positioning method, ceiling height, and how much racking and metal block line of sight. An AmIMo anchor reaches about 50 m in line of sight, indicative and site-dependent, and AmIMotion's angle of arrival works with as few as two anchors in view. As a first budget only, an open 5,000 m² hall on this site's 25 m planning grid needs about 15 anchors. AmIMotion sets the final count from a site survey. What sets the count A worked example How to get to a number Questions to ask any supplier What sets the count The task. “Which hall?” needs far fewer anchors than “which of two neighbouring lanes?”. The method. With TDoA a tag must be heard by several anchors at once: at least three for 2D and four for 3D. With two-way ranging plus angle of arrival, fewer are needed, and AmIMo anchors work with as few as two in view. Line of sight. Tall racking, machine guards, mezzanines and parked vehicles block the direct path. Aisles between high racks often need anchors that see down each aisle. Geometry. Anchors in a straight line give poor accuracy across that line. Spread them around the area where tags move. Mounting and power. AmIMo anchors go on columns, walls, ceiling structure or poles, 3 to 8 m up, and need power from a DC adapter or PoE. A worked example Take an open hall of 100 × 50 m (5,000 m²) with clear sight lines. Planned on a 25 m grid, that is 5 × 3 = 15 anchor positions. With mixed racking, a grid of about 18 m gives about 28. Dense high racking can need a grid of 12 m or less. The grids are this site's planning assumptions for a first budget, not an AmIMotion specification. Try your own floor in the anchor estimator , then let a survey set the number. How to get to a number Mark the areas where location changes a decision. Leave the rest out of scope. Write the accuracy and update rate each area needs. Note ceiling height, racking, aisles and large metal objects. Choose a positioning method per area. AmIMo anchors select the mode per zone. Lay out anchors for sight lines and geometry, then confirm with a survey and a short pilot in the hardest spot. Questions to ask any supplier Is the anchor count from a survey of my floor or a rule of thumb? What accuracy is it designed for, and where will it be worse? What cabling does each anchor need? How is accuracy measured at acceptance? AmIMotion answers each one from the site survey. Common follow-ups. Can I calculate UWB anchors from floor area? Only roughly. Area ignores racking, ceiling height, metal and the accuracy you need. Use area for a first budget, then a site survey for the plan. How far does a UWB anchor reach? An AmIMo anchor reaches about 50 m in line of sight, indicative and site-dependent. Obstructions reduce the useful range. Do UWB anchors need network cables? AmIMo anchors need no data or sync cabling: they sync over the air and send data over Wi-Fi, with an Ethernet option. Each needs power from a DC adapter or PoE, and PoE runs over a network cable. How high are anchors mounted? AmIMo anchors are mounted 3 to 8 m up, on walls, columns, ceiling structure or poles. Read next. How many anchors you need A first range, before the survey. Which job is on the trolley? A tag knows the trolley. A link knows the job. Why location needs a link to the job, and what to agree before a pilot. An RTLS tag identifies the trolley, not the job on it. To know which job is on a trolley, the system needs a carrier-to-job link: a record that this carrier holds this job, from one moment until another. In AmIMotion you link each trolley to the job it carries, in AmIHub or from your own system, and its wait then counts as that job's wait. AmIGo tags are located down to ±10 cm in 3D, depending on the site, but the radio alone never knows the job. One trolley, two identities Why a link needs a start and an end Linking in AmIHub Respect the system of record Plan for the unknown What to ask any supplier One trolley, two identities Trolley 14 has its own tag. Job 208 is what it carries today. Keeping the two apart stops a reused trolley from dragging an old job forward. AmIMotion tags the trolley and links the job. Why a link needs a start and an end A trolley carries one job, is emptied, and carries another. A link with no end would credit the second job's wait to the first. Agree who starts each link, who ends it, which event marks the change, and how mistakes get corrected. Agree those four things for AmIMotion or any other system before the pilot. Linking in AmIHub In AmIHub, work orders are objects of their own, and tags are assigned to them. You can link a trolley to its job in AmIHub, or send the link from your own system through the same interfaces AmIHub offers for everything else, REST and MQTT. How your plant links jobs today, by a scan, a record or a person, is agreed during scoping. Respect the system of record Your MES or ERP stays the authority on jobs and status. AmIHub supplies where and when. Agree the source of each field, so a location event never implies a business step. Agree up front, with AmIMotion or any supplier, that a trolley moving never changes a job's status on its own. Plan for the unknown If there is no link, a good system shows the trolley's position and says the job is unknown. If a position is old, it shows the time it was last seen. An honest partial answer beats an invented full one, and AmIMotion's map shows where each trolley was last seen, and when. What to ask any supplier Ask how jobs get linked, how links are kept and changed, which way data flows, and how mixed or split loads are handled. Then ask to see that workflow in a live demo. AmIMotion's demo on a call runs on real AmIHub data. Common follow-ups. How do I know which job is on a trolley with RTLS? Link the trolley's tag to the job it carries. In AmIMotion you make the link in AmIHub or from your own system, and AmIHub shows it with the trolley's position. Does AmIMotion track individual parts? AmIMotion tags the carrier: the trolley, bin or rack. Which parts or job it holds comes from the carrier-to-job link, not from the radio. What if one trolley carries several jobs? Agree how mixed and split loads are linked before the pilot. How AmIHub records them for your plant is settled during scoping. Does the link need our MES? No. You can link trolleys to jobs in AmIHub. Your MES or ERP can send the links later, when the pilot earns that connection. Read next. What is WIP visibility? Where each job is, and how long it waited. From zone entry to zone exit. What dwell includes, where the edge cases hide, and how AmIMotion times every wait. Dwell time is the time a tagged carrier spends inside an agreed zone, from the moment it enters to the moment it leaves. A real-time location system measures it by time-stamping every zone entry and exit. AmIMotion does this in AmIHub, with AmIGo tags located down to ±10 cm in 3D, depending on the site, so neighbouring queues and stations can be told apart. You see how long each carrier has waited while it is still waiting. Start with the zones Entry, exit and the edge What dwell includes Waits that cross a shift Using it well How AmIMotion does it Start with the zones A zone is an agreed area of the floor, such as an inspection queue or a dock lane. Draw zones around the process, not around radio coverage. In AmIHub you name the zones yourself. Neighbouring zones need positions precise enough to tell them apart, which is why UWB is used where queues sit side by side. Entry, exit and the edge Every time a tag crosses a zone boundary, AmIHub records a time. Agree what counts as a visit: a short pass through a zone on the way somewhere else should not count as waiting. A trolley parked across a boundary is the hard case. Agree a rule for it before the pilot, and ask any supplier, AmIMotion included, to show how its system handles that case. Entry 09:12 Exit still inside Waiting now 28 min Example morning, 08:00 to 12:00. Drag the trolley or the slider. What dwell includes Dwell is not cycle time. Dwell includes waiting, processing, breaks and anything else that happens while the carrier sits in the zone. To separate waiting from working you need another signal, such as a start or finish event from your MES, or a scan. AmIHub can take those events from your own systems. Waits that cross a shift A wait can start on one shift and end on the next. Before an AmIMotion pilot starts, we agree how to count a wait that runs past shift end, so every report reads the same way. Using it well Name who on your team acts when work waits too long. Compare dwell by shift, product and station, not just averages. Treat a long dwell as a reason to look, not as a diagnosis. How AmIMotion does it AmIHub time-stamps every enter, exit, idle and dwell event and keeps the history, so you can ask for time in zone by shift, station or time window. AmIHub also sends each entry and exit to any system you name, as it happens, over MQTT, REST or WebSocket. Why work waited is for your team to say. Common follow-ups. How can I see where work in progress is waiting? Tag the carriers, name the zones where work queues, and time every entry and exit. AmIHub shows how long each tagged carrier has waited in each zone. Is dwell time the same as cycle time? No. Dwell is time in a zone and includes waiting and processing. Cycle time needs process start and finish events, which AmIHub can take from your MES. Do we need an MES to measure dwell? No. Dwell comes from location and time alone. The MES link adds which job was waiting. How is a wait that runs past shift end counted? AmIMotion agrees the rule with your team before the pilot starts, so every report counts it the same way. Read next. What is WIP visibility? Where each job is, and how long it waited. Last seen, never a guess. Why tags go quiet, what the map should show, and how to check it in a pilot. When an RTLS tag is not seen for a while, the honest answer is “last seen here, at this time”, not a guess at where it is now. AmIMotion's AmIHub keeps every position with the time it was seen, so you see where each trolley was last seen, and when. AmIGo tags send as they move and sleep when still, so a quiet tag at rest is normal. Battery life is 1 to 3 years, typical and usage-dependent, and AmIHub tracks each tag's health and battery level. Why tags go quiet Freshness is its own measure What the map should show When an anchor goes dark Checking quality in a pilot Why tags go quiet The tag is still and asleep, which saves battery. AmIGo tags deep-sleep at rest and wake on motion. The tag is somewhere with poor coverage, such as inside a metal cage. The battery is low. AmIHub tracks each tag's battery level, so you can change it before it goes flat. The tag came off, or was moved to another object. If it comes off the trolley, the map still shows its last-seen spot. Freshness is its own measure How often a tag sends, how long processing takes and how often a screen refreshes are three different things. A precise point can still be too old to act on. AmIGo tags report at a rate set per tag group, from 0.1 to 10 times a second, and wake on motion. Set a freshness target for each task. What the map should show Old data shown as old. A trolley not seen for an hour should read as last seen an hour ago, in its last place, with nothing suggesting it is live. AmIMotion's map shows where each trolley was last seen, and when. When an anchor goes dark Tags are not the only thing that can go quiet. AmIHub watches the health of every AmIMo anchor and alerts when one goes dark, so a gap in coverage is found before people trust an empty area. Checking quality in a pilot Count how often tags are found where people expect them, how old positions are when people use them, and how many corrections people make. Run the count in an AmIMotion pilot before and after any change to anchors or tag rates. Common follow-ups. What happens if an RTLS tag is not seen for a while? AmIHub keeps its last position and the time it was seen, and the map shows where it was last seen. AmIMotion does not guess where the tag is now. How long do AmIGo batteries last? 1 to 3 years, typical and usage-dependent. AmIHub tracks each tag's battery level. Can a tag be moved to another trolley? Yes. Tags are assigned to objects in AmIHub, so you reassign it there. What if an anchor stops working? AmIHub monitors anchor health and alerts when an anchor goes dark. Read next. How accurate is UWB? Yes, through MCP. How an assistant reads the floor, and what keeps it in check. Yes. AmIHub, AmIMotion's location software, has a built-in MCP (Model Context Protocol) server. An MCP-capable AI assistant can ask it for live positions, zones and history from the factory floor, where AmIGo tags are located down to ±10 cm in 3D, depending on the site. Each assistant gets its own credentials and tool scope, every call is logged, and any change needs a person's approval. AmIMotion shows this in a live demo, and the setup for your site is confirmed during scoping. What MCP is What people ask The tools AmIHub describes Access, logs and approval Where it runs What MCP is Model Context Protocol is an open standard that lets AI assistants use other software in a consistent way. An MCP server describes the tools it offers, and the assistant decides when to call them. AmIHub's MCP server offers location tools. What people ask Examples of questions an assistant can answer from AmIHub: “Which forklifts have been idle for more than an hour, and where are they?” “What entered the inspection queue on the night shift?” “Where is trolley 14, and which job is on it?” The last one needs the trolley linked to its job in AmIHub. The tools AmIHub describes AmIMotion groups AmIHub's MCP tools into live location, history, zones and fences, trackables and work orders. Example tool names include get_live_locations , get_fence_events and count_idle_assets . The same tools are available over REST and MQTT. One open hub for every location system. The open standard behind interoperable industrial location, in plain words. omlox is an open standard for interoperable industrial location systems. The standard defines a common hub interface and data model, so location data from different technologies and vendors, such as UWB, BLE and RFID, can feed one location hub. AmIMotion is built on the FiRa and omlox specifications. AmIHub offers an omlox hub interface next to REST, MQTT and WebSocket, and its UWB positions reach down to ±10 cm in 3D with AmIMo anchors, depending on the site. Why omlox exists The parts And FiRa? A specification, or a certification? omlox in AmIMotion Why omlox exists Plants often end up with several location systems: RFID at the docks, BLE for one area, UWB for carriers, a fleet manager for robots. omlox lets them meet in one hub instead of one integration per vendor. A plant that adds AmIMotion can keep its other location sources in the same model. The parts omlox covers a hub that collects location data and a standard way for devices and systems to talk to it. Applications read one model of objects, zones and positions, whatever technology produced them. AmIHub's omlox hub interface is one of those standard ways in and out. And FiRa? The FiRa Consortium is an industry body that defines interoperable UWB specifications and runs certification programmes for UWB devices. FiRa covers the radio. omlox covers the location data above it. AmIMotion is built on both specifications. A specification, or a certification? Following a specification is a company's own statement. A formal certification means an authorised body has tested the product against the specification. AmIMotion describes itself as built on the FiRa and omlox specifications, and that is the claim to read. omlox in AmIMotion AmIHub has an omlox hub interface, and its data and device model follow the FiRa and omlox specifications. The same positions and events are available over REST, MQTT and WebSocket. AmIMotion keeps your location data open, whichever systems you add later. Common follow-ups. What is omlox? The FiRa Consortium defines interoperable UWB specifications and runs certification programmes for UWB devices. Do I need omlox to use AmIMotion? The baseline, before any tag goes on. What to count, how to count it fairly, and what you can claim after. Before claiming that RTLS cut search time, measure a baseline on the same flow: how often people search, how long each search takes, how far they walk, how long carriers wait in each zone and how many records need correcting. Measure it before any AmIGo tag goes on, then measure the same things with AmIMotion's live map, where positions reach down to ±10 cm in 3D, depending on the site. A fair comparison covers normal variation, such as two weeks of shifts, and reports the spread, not the best day. What to measure How to measure fairly What you can then claim A head start What to measure Searches per shift, and minutes per search. Walking distance or time to find a carrier. Time in key zones, measured by hand or from existing scans. Corrections to records, such as wrong locations or statuses. Once the AmIMotion tags are on, time in zones comes from AmIHub. Searches, walks and corrections are counted the same way as before, so before and after compare like with like. How to measure fairly Use the same flow, shifts and product mix before and after. Let the people who search record it, on a simple sheet. Two weeks is better than two days. Agree the measures with your team before the AmIMotion pilot starts. What you can then claim Compare like with like and report the spread, not just the best day. A financial case needs your real costs on top, and your team owns those numbers. In an AmIMotion pilot you see your own waits in one bay, and prove the numbers, before you decide on more. A head start The search-time calculator turns your own figures into hours a year, as a starting point for the baseline. The calculator assumes no savings, and AmIMotion never quotes one from a calculator. Common follow-ups. What should be measured before claiming RTLS reduced search time? Searches per shift, minutes per search, walking time, zone waits and record corrections, on the same flow, before tags go on. How long should a baseline run? Long enough to cover normal variation. Two weeks is a sensible minimum. Will AmIMotion calculate the financial case? Not from a calculator. A sound case needs a measured baseline and your real costs. Read next. Location you can look up, indoors. A plain guide for anyone new to real-time location on a factory floor. A real-time location system (RTLS) uses fixed receivers, called anchors, to work out where tagged objects are, usually indoors where GPS does not reach. A useful record has three parts: which object, where, and when it was seen. AmIMotion is a UWB RTLS. AmIGo tags ride on trolleys, bins and tools, AmIMo anchors hear them, and AmIHub software shows each position, down to ±10 cm in 3D with AmIMo anchors, depending on the site. How a position is made Which radio it uses What it can tell you What it cannot tell you on its own A short checklist How a position is made A tag on a trolley sends a short radio pulse as it moves. Anchors fixed on columns and walls record when the pulse arrives, and software turns those times into a position. In AmIMotion, the AmIGo tag sends the pulse. Each AmIMo anchor in range records when it arrived and, with its 3D angle-of-arrival antenna, the direction it came from. AmIHub combines timing, angle and the floor map into one position and puts it on the live map. Which radio it uses An RTLS can run on ultra-wideband (UWB), Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE), passive RFID, Wi-Fi or a mix. UWB times very short pulses, so it can tell neighbouring lanes apart. BLE is cheaper and usually works at room or zone level. RFID records a read when a tag passes an antenna. AmIMotion is built on UWB. AmIMo anchors also range BLE devices and Wi-Fi FTM devices, with device support confirmed per site. What it can tell you Where each tagged object is now, or where it was last seen. Where it went, as a trail. When it entered and left each zone, and how long it stayed. Which objects are in an area at a given time. What it cannot tell you on its own Location shows where a trolley is. Location alone does not show which job the trolley carries, whether work on it is finished, or why it is waiting. AmIMotion links each trolley to its job in AmIHub or from your own system, and the reason for a wait stays with your team. A short checklist Ask any RTLS supplier, AmIMotion included, to show five things live: the right tag on the right object, position quality in your conditions, how old each position is, how jobs are linked to carriers, and who on your team responds. The five tell you more than a moving dot on a demo screen. Common follow-ups. What does RTLS stand for? Real-time location system. AmIMotion's RTLS uses UWB tags, anchors and AmIHub software. Is RTLS the same as GPS? No. GPS uses satellites and works outdoors. An RTLS such as AmIMotion uses anchors installed in your building, so it works indoors. Which radio does an RTLS use? UWB, BLE, RFID, Wi-Fi or a mix. AmIMotion uses UWB, and the same AmIMo anchors also range BLE and Wi-Fi FTM devices, with device support confirmed per site. Does RTLS work outdoors? AmIMo anchors work indoors and in sheltered outdoor areas, such as a yard under a canopy. Read next. UWB, BLE or RFID? Choose by the question you ask. What is WIP visibility? Ask for typical accuracy and the conditions behind it, then measure it in your hardest area during a pilot. A best-case number is not an acceptance plan. What do the anchors need? Power, data cabling and sync cabling change installation time and cost in a running plant. Ask which of the three each anchor needs. Where does the data live? Ask for the interfaces, such as REST, MQTT, WebSocket and omlox, and who builds the connector. Which standards? FiRa covers UWB interoperability and omlox covers open location data. Ask whether a product follows the specification or has passed a formal certification, and read the claim as stated. Who supports it? A location system needs a survey, tuning and changes as the floor changes. Ask where the engineers are and where spares are stocked. How small can the pilot be? One bay or one line, with a baseline measured before tags go on, is usually enough to decide. One question suppliers skip Ask how the system knows which job is on a tagged trolley. UWB, BLE or RFID? Choose by the question you ask. A fair way to pick a radio for trolleys, bins and work in progress. Choose by the question your team needs answered. If you need to know that a trolley passed a gate or a station, an RFID portal or a barcode scan is often enough. If you need to know which hall or large zone it is in, BLE can do it at low cost. If you need to tell neighbouring lanes and queues apart, and see how long work waited in each, use UWB. AmIMotion is a UWB system, down to ±10 cm in 3D with AmIMo anchors, depending on the site, and the same anchors also range BLE and Wi-Fi FTM devices. What each one observes Choose by workflow Trolleys and WIP specifically Which vendors to evaluate Combining them What each one observes Barcode or QR scan. A person or a fixed scanner records an event: this carrier, at this station, at this time. Nothing is known between scans. Passive RFID (UHF). A battery-free tag is read when it passes a reader antenna, usually at a portal, a dock door or a station. Like a scan, RFID gives an event at a read point, without a person. Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE). Battery tags are heard by receivers. Signal-strength methods usually place a tag at room or zone level. Ultra-wideband (UWB). Tags and anchors time very short radio pulses (IEEE 802.15.4z). The result is a continuous position, precise enough to tell neighbouring lanes and queue positions apart. UWB infrastructure costs more than BLE, and anchors are planned from a site survey. Choose by workflow The question your team asks What usually fits Did this trolley reach the station or leave through the gate? Barcode scan or RFID portal Which hall or large zone is this bin in? BLE Which of two neighbouring queues is this job in, and in what order? UWB How long did this work wait between operations? UWB, or scans at every boundary if people scan every time Where are forklifts and AMRs relative to loads? UWB Trolleys and WIP specifically A tag on a trolley tells you where the trolley is, not which job it holds. For WIP visibility you also need a link between carrier and job. The same holds for every technology on this page, AmIMotion included. Scans and RFID already give events where work changes hands. The gap is usually the time in between: work waiting beside a cell, or in a queue nobody scans. Continuous UWB position from AmIMotion earns its cost in that gap. Which vendors to evaluate For UWB, plants look at global suppliers and Indian makers. AmIMotion, in Bengaluru, is an Indian maker of UWB tags, anchors and software. The guide to UWB RTLS in India lists suppliers and the questions to ask. For RFID and BLE there are many reader and tag makers. Ask every vendor, AmIMotion included, the same three questions: accuracy measured how, what the infrastructure needs, and how a job gets linked to a carrier. Combining them These are not rivals. Keep scans where the process already needs them, and add continuous location only where work goes quiet. AmIMo anchors also range BLE devices and Wi-Fi FTM devices, so one AmIMotion installation can serve more than one kind of device, with device support confirmed per site. Common follow-ups. Is UWB more accurate than BLE? Generally, yes. UWB times very short pulses, while most BLE systems estimate distance from signal strength. AmIMotion's UWB reaches down to ±10 cm in 3D with AmIMo anchors. Real accuracy for either depends on the site. Is RFID enough to track WIP? For events at fixed read points, often yes. RFID does not show position or waiting time between readers unless you add more read points. Can one system read UWB and BLE tags? Some can. AmIMo anchors range UWB, BLE and Wi-Fi FTM from the same unit, with device support confirmed per site. When is UWB worth the extra cost? Where work waits between read points and people walk to find it. Where a scan at each step already answers the question, a scan may be enough. Read next. Scan, checkpoint or location? What is WIP visibility? Where each job is, and how long it waited. What it means, what it needs, and where a plant should start. WIP (work-in-progress) visibility means knowing where each job physically is and how long it has waited at each step. WIP tracking shows where a carrier is. Visibility adds which job the carrier holds and its time in each zone. AmIMotion builds it from three parts: AmIGo tags on trolleys and bins, AmIMo anchors that locate them down to ±10 cm in 3D, depending on the site, and AmIHub software, where each carrier is linked to its job and every zone entry and exit is time-stamped. Three things it needs What it tells you What it cannot tell you How to start Three things it needs A tag on the carrier. The trolley, bin or rack carries its own AmIGo tag. A reliable position. AmIMo anchors locate the tag, and every reading carries its time. UWB can tell neighbouring queues apart. A link to the job. Each trolley is linked to the job it carries, in AmIHub or from your own system. What it tells you Where a job is, where it has been, when it entered each zone and how long it has waited, while it is still waiting. In AmIMotion, supervisors see each wait live during the shift, not at the next morning's review. A long wait is a reason for a named person to go and look. What it cannot tell you Being in a zone does not prove work started or finished. A long wait does not explain why. Location never authorises an action by itself. AmIMotion leaves the reason for a wait with your team. How to start Ask one question first: which part of the flow makes people walk the floor to find out what is happening? Tag that flow's trolleys, agree a few zones, and name who acts when work waits too long. Measure how work is found before and after. AmIMotion starts with one bay or one line. Common follow-ups. What is the difference between WIP visibility and WIP tracking? Tracking shows where a carrier is. Visibility adds which job it holds and how long it waited in each zone. AmIMotion adds the job through a link in AmIHub. Which companies offer real-time WIP tracking for manufacturing? Several RTLS suppliers do. AmIMotion, from Bengaluru, starts with WIP visibility in manufacturing, using UWB down to ±10 cm in 3D, depending on the site. Where should a plant start? With one flow where people walk to find work, such as machining to assembly, in one bay or one line. Does WIP visibility mean tagging every part? No. AmIMotion tags the carrier: the trolley, bin or rack. The job it holds comes from the carrier-to-job link. Read next. How waits are timed From zone entry to zone exit. This notice covers the amimotion.com website. It says what the site collects, what it does not, and what you can ask of us. The AmIMotion website has no sign-up, no advertising trackers and no analytics. The planning tools and Plan your first bay run in your browser. Your answers to Plan your first bay sit in this browser tab only, and nothing reaches AmIMotion until you send an email. When you write to us, Locatepro Technologies Pvt Ltd uses your details to reply and to follow up the enquiry you started. You can ask to see, correct or erase them under India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023. Trust and data · People and privacy Who we are This website is run by Locatepro Technologies Pvt Ltd, Bengaluru, India. AmIMotion is its brand. For personal data you send us through this site, we are the Data Fiduciary under India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023. Write to us at sales@amimotion.com . What the site does not do There is no sign-up and no account. The site sets no cookies. It loads no advertising, analytics or social-media trackers. It loads no fonts or scripts from other companies' servers. What stays in your browser Plan your first bay keeps your answers in this browser tab, so you can go back a step. They are deleted when you close the tab, and Start over clears them at once. If you type a work email there, the page guesses your company name from it inside your browser. How many anchors you need , Time spent searching and Your pilot on one page work out their answers in your browser and keep nothing. A brief you download is a file on your own device. Copy puts text on your own clipboard. When you send us something The contact form and Plan your first bay open a draft email in your own mail app, addressed to sales@amimotion.com. Nothing reaches us until you press send. When you do, we receive what the email contains: usually your name, work email and company, your role and phone number if you gave them, and your answers. We use it only to reply to you and to follow up the enquiry you started. We do not sell it, and we do not add you to a newsletter. How long we keep it We keep an enquiry for as long as we need it to reply and to follow up, then erase it, unless a law requires us to keep it longer. Server logs The company that hosts this site may record standard request data, such as your IP address, browser type, the page asked for and the time, to serve the site and keep it secure. We do not use it to build a profile of you. Your rights Under the DPDP Act you can ask us for a summary of the personal data we hold about you and how we use it. You can ask us to correct, complete, update or erase it. You can name someone to act for you if you die or cannot act yourself. You can withdraw your consent at any time, as easily as you gave it, by writing to us. Withdrawing does not undo what was lawfully done before. Complaints Write to sales@amimotion.com first, and we will answer you. If you are not satisfied with our answer, you may complain to the Data Protection Board of India. Children This site is for businesses. It is not meant for children, and we do not knowingly collect a child's personal data. Other sites A link to another website, such as a video channel, takes you to that site's own privacy terms. Changes If this notice changes, the new version goes on this page with its date. AmIMotion is a UWB location system in three parts. AmIGo tags use IEEE 802.15.4z HRP radio on channels 5 and 9 and report 0.1 to 10 times a second. AmIMo anchors time each pulse, read its 3D angle of arrival and need only DC or PoE power. AmIHub places tags down to ±10 cm in 3D with AmIMo anchors, depending on your floor, and runs inside your plant or in the cloud. AmIMotion is built on the FiRa and omlox specifications. Which positioning methods does AmIMotion use? Several, chosen per zone in AmIHub: UL-TDoA, DL-TDoA, two-way ranging and 3D angle of arrival. Most asset tracking uses UL-TDoA, where AmIGo tags send and AmIMo anchors time the pulse. What update rate do AmIGo tags support? 0.1 to 10 Hz, set per tag group. AmIGo tags sleep when still and send when they move, which is why one battery lasts 1 to 3 years, typical. How accurate is AmIMotion? Down to ±10 cm in 3D, typical, with AmIMo anchors. It depends on your floor, so you measure it on yours in the pilot, near racking and machines too. Why are size and weight not listed? A tag sends a pulse a few nanoseconds long. Anchors note when it arrives and where it came from. AmIHub works out the spot. AmIMotion locates tags with ultra-wideband (UWB) radio, to IEEE 802.15.4z. An AmIGo tag sends a pulse a few nanoseconds long. Each AmIMo anchor in range records its time of arrival and its angle of arrival. AmIHub compares the times between anchors (time difference of arrival, TDoA) and the angles, and works out a 3D position. With AmIMo anchors that is down to ±10 cm, typical. How close depends on your floor. AmIMotion is built on the FiRa and omlox specifications. Positioning modes · Specifications Light travels about 30 cm in a nanosecond. So the time a pulse takes to reach each anchor says how far it went. Small timing differences between anchors become a position. Time Each AmIMo anchor records when the pulse arrives. The differences between anchors place the tag. This is time difference of arrival, TDoA. Angle An antenna array in each AmIMo reads the direction the pulse came from, side to side and up and down. So fewer anchors fix a position, and height counts. The map AmIHub combines the times, the angles and your floor map into one 3D position, stamped with the time it was seen. Steel and racking. What they do to the signal. Steel and racking bounce radio around a hall. Each echo arrives a little after the direct signal. A UWB pulse is so short that the direct signal and its echoes arrive apart, so AmIMo can tell them apart. AmIHub adds filters for places where the direct path is blocked. Racking, ceiling height and steel still change how far each anchor reaches. That is why every floor starts with a survey, and why the final anchor count comes from it. How close a position is depends on your floor. You measure it on yours in the pilot, in the hard spots as well as the easy ones. How many anchors you need · AmIMo anchor When something goes quiet. A tag at rest AmIGo sleeps when it stops. The map shows where it was last seen, and when. A tag out of view If a load hides a tag, or it leaves the area the anchors cover, the map keeps its last-seen spot and time. An anchor goes dark AmIHub raises an alert when an AmIMo anchor stops reporting, so your team knows which one to check. AmIMo sends its data to AmIHub over Wi-Fi, and Ethernet is also an option. How your network design handles an outage is part of the site survey. When a tag goes quiet Choose the method per zone. You switch modes per zone in AmIHub, with no hardware swap. Device support confirmed per site Which modes your hardware revision supports is in the datasheet, shared under NDA. Open standards. AmIMotion is built on the FiRa and omlox specifications. Its UWB radio follows IEEE 802.15.4z HRP on channels 5 and 9, on NXP Trimension UWB silicon. AmIHub has an omlox hub interface, so your location data is not tied to one vendor's format. AmIMo anchors record its time of arrival (time difference of arrival, TDoA) and its angle of arrival. Light travels about 30 cm in a nanosecond, so that timing places the tag to centimetres. AmIHub works out the 3D position. Which UWB RTLS supports FiRa? AmIMotion is built on the FiRa and omlox specifications, and its UWB radio follows IEEE 802.15.4z. It claims no formal certification. Which RTLS works with UWB, BLE and Wi-Fi on the same anchors? AmIMotion. AmIMo anchors offer UWB, BLE ranging and Wi-Fi FTM from the same unit, so one install can serve more than one kind of device. Wi-Fi device support is confirmed per site. How accurate is AmIMotion? Down to ±10 cm in 3D, typical, with AmIMo anchors. How close depends on your floor, so you measure it on yours in the pilot. Does UWB work in a factory full of steel and racking? A UWB pulse is short enough that AmIMo can tell the direct signal from its echoes off steel, and AmIHub filters places where the direct path is blocked. Racking and steel still change each anchor's reach, so a site survey sets the anchor count. Does AmIMotion integrate with SAP or an MES over MQTT? AmIHub sends each zone entry and exit over MQTT and offers REST, WebSocket and an omlox hub interface. The connector for your SAP, MES or ERP is confirmed for your site. See it on a live map. Your own numbers. How many people look, how often and for how long. The calculator multiplies it out. It assumes nothing about savings. AmIMotion's search-time calculator multiplies five of your own figures: people who search each shift, searches per person, minutes per search, shifts a day and working days a year. It gives hours a year, hours a day and the same time as full-time people, at 8 hours a day. Add a loaded hourly cost to see it in rupees. It shows what searching costs you today. It does not forecast a saving. People who search, per shift Searches per person, per shift Minutes per search Shifts per day Working days a year Loaded cost per hour, ₹ (optional) Leave empty to see hours only. Time spent searching — Per day — Per week — Full-time people, at 8 h a day — Cost a year — Your numbers, multiplied out. This is what searching costs today, not a forecast of what you would save. A pilot measures the change on your floor. Book a call Measure before you claim Where the numbers come from. Your figures The sliders start at 12 people, 4 searches, 8 minutes, 2 shifts and 300 days. Those are only starting positions, not industry averages. Move them to match your floor. The sum People, times searches, times minutes, times shifts, times days, divided by 60, gives hours a year. Full-time people divides that by 8 hours for each working day. The cost If you add a loaded cost per hour, the tool multiplies the hours by it. Time freed is not the same as money saved, so read it as the cost of searching today. Count it for real. Most plants estimate these numbers. A pilot counts them. Before it starts, time how long it takes to find the trolleys in one flow. Then AmIMotion tags them. An AmIGo tag rides on each trolley, and AmIHub's live map shows where it was last seen, and when. You find out from a screen, not a walk. Time the same searches again with the map open. That difference, on your floor, is the number you can defend. Measure before you claim · Where is that trolley? Where your data lives. AmIHub can run inside your plant with no internet needed. This page says who can read what, and what each claim on this site rests on. AmIMotion's AmIHub runs on an industrial PC inside your plant, with no internet needed, or in the cloud. Every interface uses TLS. You set who sees what, by role. Each system and AI assistant gets its own API key and scope, and every request is logged. You set how long the map keeps its history. The figures on this site, such as down to ±10 cm with AmIMo anchors, come from AmIMotion's own published specifications and depend on your floor. For developers · People and privacy Where it runs. Inside your plant AmIHub runs on an industrial PC inside your plant, with no internet needed. Positions, zones and history do not have to leave your network. In the cloud AmIHub can also run in the cloud. The same access controls, audit logs and history settings apply in both. Who can read it. Encrypted in transit AmIHub uses TLS on every interface, from REST and MQTT to the MCP server. Access by role You set who sees what, by role. Each system and each AI assistant gets its own API key and scope. Every request logged AmIHub keeps an audit log. For an AI assistant, it records who asked, what was called and what changed. History you set You also set how long the map keeps its history. A person approves changes Asking changes nothing. Any change, such as raising a work order in AmIHub, needs a person's approval. You can require it from a supervisor. We show it live on a call. Ask your floor . Firmware over the air AmIHub updates anchor and tag firmware over the air. What the claims rest on. Every figure on this site has a source and a condition. Product figures They come from AmIMotion's own published specifications and are indicative. Down to ±10 cm needs AmIMo anchors and depends on your floor. A battery life of 1 to 3 years depends on use. Final datasheets are shared under NDA. Standards AmIMotion is built on the FiRa and omlox specifications. It claims no formal certification. What a position cannot tell you A position does not show which job a trolley carries until the job is linked to it . It does not show that work is done, or why it waited. Those need your links, your zones and your team. Customers This site names no customer and shows no customer result. Questions teams ask first. Does AmIHub need the internet? No. AmIHub runs on an industrial PC inside your plant, with no internet needed. It can also run in the cloud. Can an AI assistant change anything in AmIHub? Asking changes nothing. Each assistant gets its own access: read-only, or only the actions you allow. Any change, such as raising a work order, needs a person's approval, and you can require it from a supervisor. Every request it makes is logged. AmIMotion shows it live on a call. Does AmIMotion hold a formal certification? AmIMotion is built on the FiRa and omlox specifications. It claims no formal certification. Does the pilot track people? No. The AmIMotion pilot tags trolleys, bins and pallets, not people. Tagging people would be a separate project. The tag goes on the trolley. An AmIMotion pilot follows work, not workers. Here is what it tags, what the map shows and who decides. An AmIMotion pilot tags trolleys, bins and pallets, not people. The AmIGo tag goes on the trolley, not on the person pushing it. AmIHub's map shows where tagged things are and how long they have waited. Tagging people would be a separate project. It would need its own policy. You set who sees what, by role, and how long the map keeps its history. What the map shows. AmIHub shows where each tagged trolley, bin or pallet is, and how long it has waited in a zone. It shows where a tag was last seen, and when. In the AmIMotion pilot, no person carries a tag. So no person is on the map, and the map does not show who pushed a trolley. Why it waited is for your team to say. A long wait shows where to look in the flow. It does not say who is to blame. Who sees what. Access by role You set who sees what, by role. Each system and each AI assistant gets its own access, and every request is logged. Trust and data . History you set You also set how long the map keeps its history. Inside your plant AmIHub can run on an industrial PC inside your plant, with no internet needed. If you ever want to tag people. It is never part of an AmIMotion WIP pilot. Tagging people would be a separate project, outside the pilot. It would need its own policy. Talk to us about it before anything is tagged. How a pilot runs . In India, a location tied to a named person is personal data under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023. Your own policy would need to cover it. Privacy . Questions teams ask first. Does AmIMotion track workers? The AmIMotion pilot tags trolleys, bins and pallets, not people. The tag goes on the trolley, not on the person pushing it. Tagging people would be a separate project. It would need its own policy. Can a supervisor see who moved a trolley? No. The map shows where the trolley went and when. No person carries a tag in the pilot, so the map does not show who pushed it. Who decides how long the history is kept? You do. You set how long the map keeps its history. Does a tag on a forklift track its driver? Forklifts are not part of the WIP pilot. If you tag vehicles later, the map shows the vehicle, and your policy decides how that history is used. Bring the hard questions to the call. Ask who sees what, and how long it is kept. AmIMotion answers on the call, with AmIHub open. Book a call Where work is. Where it waits. AmIMotion is a Bengaluru company that makes spatial intelligence for factories and warehouses. Its AmIGo tags ride on trolleys, bins, tools and vehicles. Its AmIMo anchors hear each tag's ultra-wideband (UWB) signal. Its AmIHub software shows on one live map where work is and how long it has waited, down to ±10 cm in 3D with AmIMo anchors, depending on the floor. AmIMotion is a brand of Locatepro Technologies Pvt Ltd. It designs and builds its tags and anchors in India. How it works · About us What AmIMotion does Who it is for How it starts Who leads it The name What AmIMotion is not Facts, with their conditions What AmIMotion does AmIMotion answers two questions a plant asks every shift: where is it, and how long has it waited. Find it. A tagged trolley, bin, tool or forklift shows on AmIHub 's live map, with where it was last seen, and when. You find out from a screen, not a walk. See where work waits. AmIHub notes when each tagged carrier enters and leaves a zone you name. Link a trolley to the job it carries, and its wait counts as that job's wait. Ask your floor. AmIHub has an MCP server built in, so AI assistants can ask the live map a question. Asking changes nothing. Any change needs a person's approval. Vehicles on the same map. Forklifts, tuggers and AGVs carry vehicle tags and share the same anchors. Who it is for Manufacturing and warehouse teams who walk the floor to find out what is happening: plant heads, production control, industrial engineering and lean leads, supervisors and line-side logistics, and the OT, IT and MES teams who connect floor data to MES, ERP and WMS. How it starts A pilot follows one flow in one bay or line. You see your own waits in that bay, and prove the numbers, before you decide on more. Then AmIMotion grows plant-wide on the same AmIHub, without re-fitting the first bay. How a pilot runs . Who leads it AmIMotion is led by Kaushal Kukkar, founder and CEO, and Vivek Dham, CTO. Its tags and anchors are designed and built in India on NXP Trimension UWB silicon, with local stock and local engineers on your site. The name Say it "Ammy-Motion". It is written with a capital A, I and M. The products share the prefix: AmIGo , the tag; AmIMo , the anchor; AmIHub, the software. What AmIMotion is not AmIMotion is an industrial UWB indoor positioning company in Bengaluru, India. It is not a video or presentation maker, and not an AI video tool with a similar name. It locates tagged trolleys, bins, tools and vehicles on an indoor floor. Facts, with their conditions AmIMotion is a brand of Locatepro Technologies Pvt Ltd, Bengaluru, India. Contact: sales@amimotion.com. Category: Industrial Spatial Intelligence. Commercial focus: WIP (work-in-progress) visibility in manufacturing. Foundation: UWB real-time location (RTLS). The system has three parts: AmIGo UWB tags, AmIMo UWB anchors and AmIHub software. Positioning: down to ±10 cm in 3D, with AmIMo anchors. Accuracy depends on the site and is measured in a pilot. Radios: UWB, BLE and Wi-Fi FTM on the same anchors. Built on NXP Trimension UWB silicon.
